content:
Let \(s(n)\) be the squarefree part of \(n\). Then a triple has square product iff the product of their squarefree parts is a square, i.e. one squarefree part is the product of the other two.

For \(\{1,\dots,15\}\), the squarefree parts are:
\[
1:\{1,4,9\},\quad 2:\{2,8\},\quad 3:\{3,12\},\quad 5,6,7,10,11,13,14,15 \text{ once each}.
\]
Among the nonzero kernels, the only bad triples are
\[
\{2,3,6\},\{2,5,10\},\{2,7,14\},\{3,5,15\},\{6,10,15\}.
\]

The kernels \(11,13\) are in no bad triple, so they can always be included. Among the other eight, at most six can be chosen: if \(2\) is chosen, at most one from each pair \(\{3,6\},\{5,10\},\{7,14\}\), plus possibly \(15\), giving at most \(5\); if \(2\) is not chosen, the remaining seven cannot all be chosen because \(\{3,5,15\}\) and \(\{6,10,15\}\) would both appear. Thus at most \(8\) nonzero kernels can be chosen, and
\[
\{3,5,6,7,10,11,13,14\}
\]
achieves \(8\).

Now let \(q\) be the number of chosen elements with squarefree part \(1\), i.e. from \(\{1,4,9\}\).

- \(q=3\) is impossible since \(1\cdot4\cdot9=36\) is a square.
- If \(q=2\), no nonzero kernel can appear twice, or two such elements plus one square would form a square. Thus the total is at most \(2+8=10\).
- If \(q=1\), similarly the total is at most \(1+8=9\).
- If \(q=0\), choosing \(11\) or more non-squares would leave at most one nonzero kernel type absent, so not all five bad triples above could be destroyed; hence at most \(10\) elements.

The bound is attained by
\[
\{1,4,3,5,6,7,10,11,13,14\}.
\]
Its nonzero kernels avoid all five bad triples, and it contains only two square-kernel elements.

Thus the largest possible subset has size
\[
\boxed{10}.
\]
